details: Peter M. Aronow and Joel A. Middleton. A Class of Unbiased Estimators of the Average Treatment Effect in Randomized Experiments. Journal of Causal Inference 1(1), 135-154, 2013. DOI 10.1515/jci-2012-0009 (IDEAS/RePEc page). Abstract (paraphrased from fetch): design-based estimators of the ATE that are unbiased when the assignment mechanism is known, extended to unbiased covariate adjustment with any analyst-chosen outcome model, with variance formulas and conservative variance estimators.
bears_on: C1: design-based exactly unbiased covariate-adjusted estimator with an arbitrary fitted model, the randomization-inference analogue of a difference estimator with a fitted coefficient.

details: Changbao Wu and Randy R. Sitter. A Model-calibration Approach to Using Complete Auxiliary Information from Survey Data. Journal of the American Statistical Association 96, 185-193, March 2001 (citation verified from Wu's Waterloo publication list and an IDEAS reference record). Abstract not retrieved.
bears_on: C1 and C0: model-calibration estimators that use a fitted, possibly nonlinear assisting model under the design; relevant to a difference estimator with an estimated coefficient. Abstract not seen.

details: Fangzhou Su and Peng Ding. Model-assisted analyses of cluster-randomized experiments. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 83(5), 994-1015, November 2021. DOI 10.1111/rssb.12468 (IDEAS page; note pages are 994-1015, not 904-927). arXiv:2104.04647. Abstract (paraphrased): design-based view with only assignment random and no outcome model; regression on cluster totals is consistent and more efficient with many clusters; covariates improve efficiency with a trade-off against robustness; robust standard errors approximate the true asymptotic standard errors; extended to weighted average treatment effects.
bears_on: C1 and C12: design-based cluster-level covariate adjustment and its efficiency; asymptotics are in the number of clusters, so it says little about few clusters or fpc.

details: T. L. Kennel and R. Valliant. Robust variance estimators for generalized regression estimators in cluster samples. Survey Methodology 45(3), December 2019 (Statistics Canada 12-001-X). Pages and abstract not shown on the page the fetch tool returned. Introduction text states that linearization may not converge fast enough in small to moderate samples and that popular methods tend to underestimate true sampling errors. Related dissertation: Kennel, Topics in Model-Assisted Point and Variance Estimation in Clustered Samples, University of Maryland, 2013, advisor Valliant (leverage-adjusted sandwich variance for GREG in two-stage samples).
bears_on: C9: leverage-adjusted (CR2/BRL-like) variance estimation for GREG in cluster samples; the survey-side counterpart to cluster-robust small-sample corrections.

details: Two candidates. (1) E. L. Korn and B. I. Graubard. Simultaneous Testing of Regression Coefficients with Complex Survey Data: Use of Bonferroni t Statistics. The American Statistician 44(4), 270-276, 1990 (RTI publication page). Abstract: Wald tests need a consistent covariance estimate; NHANES II design allows at most 32 degrees of freedom; Bonferroni t statistics proposed as an alternative. (2) A Survey Methodology paper titled Confidence intervals for proportions with small expected number of positive counts estimated from survey data appeared in search results under catalogue code 12-001-X19980024356 (issue 1998002); the authors, volume and pages were not verified and the page fetch returned a site-unavailable notice. Which one the seed means was not resolved. The book Analysis of Health Surveys (Korn and Graubard 1999) was not looked up.
bears_on: C9: t reference with design degrees of freedom limited by the number of PSUs, and effective-df confidence intervals for survey estimates with few PSUs.

details: Title confirmed as Degrees of freedom approximations and rules-of-thumb (ISR record api.isr.umich.edu/?p=191256 and RTI listings). The page shows a Statistics Sweden copyright line and does not give authors, volume or pages, so the seed's Journal of Official Statistics 2010 attribution is unverified by me. Abstract (paraphrased): the common rule df = number of PSUs minus number of strata performs poorly in some situations; a simple alternative df estimate improves confidence interval coverage.
bears_on: C9: degrees of freedom for t intervals with few PSUs, the survey-sampling analogue of Satterthwaite or Bell-McCaffrey df.

details: Robert M. Bell and Daniel F. McCaffrey. Bias reduction in standard errors for linear regression with multi-stage samples. Survey Methodology, 2002 issue 2 (Statistics Canada catalogue 12-001-X20020029058, released 29 January 2003); volume and pages not stated on the catalogue page. Abstract (paraphrased): linearization works with many PSUs but can substantially underestimate variance with few PSUs or when a coefficient depends on a few PSUs; proposes bias-reduced linearization using adjusted residuals, unbiased under iid errors; suggests a Satterthwaite df approximation; the jackknife is biased upward in these cases. A RAND external publication page also exists for a linear and GLM version (not opened).
bears_on: C9: origin of CR2 and Bell-McCaffrey df in the survey setting with few PSUs.

details: Guido W. Imbens and Michal Kolesar. Robust standard errors in small samples: Some practical advice. Review of Economics and Statistics 98(4), 701-712, October 2016. DOI 10.1162/REST_a_00552 (Princeton record). NBER Working Paper 18478. Abstract (paraphrased): Bell-McCaffrey df correction arises from the Behrens-Fisher problem; an improvement for clustered data; coverage improves even with fifty or more clusters; recommends routinely computing the adjustment.
bears_on: C9: Bell-McCaffrey df and CR2 for cluster-robust confidence intervals; applicable to the cluster-robust PPI interval.

details: James E. Pustejovsky and Elizabeth Tipton. Small-Sample Methods for Cluster-Robust Variance Estimation and Hypothesis Testing in Fixed Effects Models. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 36(4), 672-683, October 2018. DOI 10.1080/07350015.2016.1247004 (IDEAS page). arXiv:1601.01981. Abstract (paraphrased): CRVE is biased downward with few clusters; generalizes bias-reduced linearization to arbitrary fixed effects with Satterthwaite t tests and a multi-parameter small-sample test; R package clubSandwich.
bears_on: C9: CR2 with Satterthwaite df as the standard small-sample cluster-robust recipe.

details: A. Colin Cameron, Jonah B. Gelbach and Douglas L. Miller. Bootstrap-based improvements for inference with clustered errors. Review of Economics and Statistics 90(3), 414-427, August 2008. DOI 10.1162/rest.90.3.414 (volume and issue are from the DOI string as read by the fetch tool). Abstract (paraphrased): with about 5 to 30 clusters standard cluster-robust tests over-reject; cluster bootstrap-t (wild cluster) procedures give asymptotic refinement; nominal 5% restored from about 10%.
bears_on: C9: wild cluster bootstrap for few clusters.

details: Nina Hagesaether and Li-Chun Zhang. A Note on the Effect of Auxiliary Information on the Variance of Cluster Sampling. Journal of Official Statistics 25(3), 397-404, 2009 (bibliographic details as printed on the PDF at scb.se; a Statistics Norway repository page lists the same paper with a different volume and issue, 21(4), which I took to be a page error). Abstract as printed: model-based synthesis of design-effect results for cluster sampling; auxiliary information removes the extra variance due to variation in cluster sizes and reduces efficiency loss to the extent it reduces the conditional intra-cluster correlation given the covariates; the design effect depends on the remaining conditional ICC and average cluster size.
bears_on: C12: design effect of a regression/GREG estimator under cluster sampling is governed by the conditional ICC, the same quantity as 1 - R^2_cluster at the cluster level.

details: Found the MDRC report: Howard S. Bloom, Lashawn Richburg-Hayes and Alison Rebeck Black. Using Covariates to Improve Precision: Empirical Guidance for Studies That Randomize Schools to Measure the Impacts of Educational Interventions. MDRC, November 2005 (mdrc.org/node/14682). Abstract (paraphrased): pretests, especially school-level pretests, raise precision in school-randomized trials; the number of schools needed falls to about half for elementary, one-fifth for middle and one-tenth for high schools. I could not confirm the Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis 2007 journal version (the seed's citation); the sagepub DOI fetch was blocked and the MDRC page does not mention it.
bears_on: C12: cluster-level covariate R^2 and precision gains when whole clusters are the unit of assignment or labelling.
